The Real Gold Rush: Expanding the Surface

Onwards and upwards!

⚛️ Trump’s Saudi Nuke Deal: Treaty by Pen, Conditions by Post

Yesterday, Trump signed a 30‑year civil nuclear pact with Saudi Arabia that lets US companies build reactors and, after a joint feasibility study, potentially an enrichment facility on Saudi soil. 

Today, he jumped on social media and announced that the whole thing is “totally subject” to Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords, with “no enrichment” allowed and only “Civil (Non‑Enriched) Nuclear Facilities” approved. 

The text gives Saudi Arabia a path to enrichment; the president’s feed pretends it doesn’t — and makes Israel the gatekeeper after the signature, not before.

On paper, this is the deal Trump’s own team spent a year separating from recognition of Israel. The 123 Agreement reportedly drops the UAE‑style “gold standard”: no blanket ban on enrichment, no mandatory Additional Protocol, no explicit renunciation clause. 

It positions US firms at the center of Saudi civil nuclear development and allows a US‑built enrichment facility if a joint US–Saudi study says so — exactly the kind of scheduled mechanism nonproliferation experts warned would weaken guardrails in the middle of a war against Iran’s nuclear program. 

Now the same president who delinked nuclear talks from normalization in 2025 is trying to relink them, not by renegotiating the treaty, but by declaring that “if they don’t join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off.”

For Riyadh, this is classic American theater. Saudi officials have said for years they won’t normalize with Israel without a credible path to Palestinian statehood — something Netanyahu’s government flatly rejects. 

The kingdom just locked in a signed path to reactors and potential enrichment under US technology; it now watches Trump retro‑fit a political condition whose logic was precisely what his negotiators stripped out. For Israel, it’s a weird victory lap. 

Netanyahu’s office calls Saudi entry into the Abraham Accords an “historic leap,” while Energy Minister Eli Cohen publicly frets that if Washington walks away, Riyadh will simply buy its civilian nukes from China, where oversight is weaker. 

Officially, Israel backs the pressure. Quietly, it knows the hard question is not “if” there will be enrichment, but “under what conditions, and who will have oversight” — the space where Trump’s tweet and the pact diverge.

The real story isn’t about a bomb tomorrow. Between enriched uranium and a weapon lies an industry Saudi Arabia does not yet have. It’s about status and control. 

The UAE accepted no enrichment and intrusive inspections to get US reactors. Saudi Arabia just got a softer deal in writing and a harder narrative online. On the legal side, the gold standard stopped at the Saudi border. 

On the political side, Trump is trying to resurrect it as a loyalty test to Israel — editing a signed agreement from his feed, while Congress and Riyadh are left to guess which version of US policy is real.

Who runs nonproliferation in this “new Middle East”: the lawyers who drafted the pact, the president doing nuclear policy by post, or the crown prince who just secured a path to enrichment and can wait out both?

🤖 The AI investment race is not only a technology story

It is also a capital-allocation story.

A new BIS working paper models the current AI build-out as a race for a small number of dominant market positions.

The result is uncomfortable.

Under the paper’s conservative baseline, firms overinvest by roughly 50% relative to the socially efficient level. Under weaker demand conditions, that gap can rise to around three times the efficient level.

Why?

Because every company faces the same pressure:

Invest early.
Build capacity first.
Secure the market before someone else does.

That can produce:

• duplicated infrastructure
• debt-funded expansion
• circular financial relationships
• specialised assets that are difficult to resell
• larger losses if revenue expectations fail

The paper does not argue that AI lacks economic value.

It argues that real technological value does not guarantee efficient capital allocation.

A transformative technology can still create an unstable investment cycle.

For markets, the useful question is not only:

“How powerful is the technology?”

It is also:

“How much capital already depends on the most optimistic outcome?”

Capability explains the opportunity.
The balance sheet explains the fragility.

Source: BIS Working Paper No. 1367, The AI Investment Race, 14 July 2026.
